titleEn: Let the redeemed of the LORD say so
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Gm | Dm A | Dm Dm |
intro: Forty three verses that open Book Five of the psalms, built out of four rescue stories told in the same shape: people in trouble, a shout, a rescue, a call to give thanks. Wanderers in the desert, prisoners in irons, the sick, and sailors in a storm. Two refrains hold it together, the cry at verses 6, 13, 19 and 28 and the thanksgiving at verses 8, 15, 21 and 31, so a learner who reads those eight verses first will recognise most of the vocabulary of the rest. The last eleven verses drop the refrain and turn into a hymn about reversal, water into desert and desert into water. Watch the word for covenant kindness: it is the last word of verse 1 and the second to last of verse 43, and everything in between is what it looks like in practice.

stichs.en: Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good,
for His kindness is forever.

verses.summary: The same opening line stands at the head of Psalms 106, 118 and 136. The claim is made flat, before any story is told to support it.

stichs.en: Let the redeemed of the LORD say it,
those He redeemed from the hand of an adversary,

verses.summary: The thanks is assigned to a named group rather than to everyone. The next forty verses are the answer to who these people are.

stichs.en: and whom He gathered in from the lands,
from east and from west, from north and from the sea.

verses.summary: Four directions, and the fourth is the sea rather than the south. That is how a writer on this coastline says every direction at once.

stichs.en: They wandered in the wilderness, on a wasteland road;
a city to live in they did not find.

verses.summary: The first of the four stories. The trouble is not danger but disorientation: a road going nowhere and nothing at the end of it.

stichs.en: Hungry and thirsty too,
their soul grew faint inside them.

verses.summary: The body is named before the inner state it produces. The soul does not collapse on its own; hunger and thirst wear it down first.

stichs.en: Then they cried out to the LORD in the distress that was theirs;
from their straits He rescued them.

verses.summary: The first appearance of the refrain that runs the psalm. No repentance is mentioned and no merit is claimed. They shout, and that is the whole condition.

stichs.en: He set them walking on a straight road,
to reach a city to live in.

verses.summary: The rescue answers verse 4 phrase by phrase: a straight road instead of a wasteland track, a city to settle in instead of none.

stichs.en: Let them thank the LORD for His kindness,
and for His wonders toward the children of humankind.

verses.summary: The second refrain, the one that answers rescue. The verb is a jussive, someone urging: gratitude is being asked for, not reported.

stichs.en: For He satisfied a craving soul,
and a hungry soul He filled with good.

verses.summary: The reason clause behind the refrain. Craving and hunger are answered by satisfying and filling, and what is given is named simply as good.

stichs.en: Those who sat in darkness and deepest gloom,
prisoners of affliction and iron,

verses.summary: The second story. These are not lost travellers but captives, and the pair of words for their darkness is the one the psalms keep for the edge of death.

stichs.en: because they defied the words of God,
and spurned the counsel of the Most High.

verses.summary: Unlike the wanderers, this group is given a cause. The psalm is willing to say that some trouble is earned.

stichs.en: He bent their heart down with hard labour;
they stumbled, and there was no one to help.

verses.summary: The humbling is God's own act. That makes the release that follows a reversal by the same hand, not a rescue from someone else.

stichs.en: Then they cried out to the LORD in the distress that was theirs;
from their straits He saved them.

verses.summary: The refrain returns with two verbs swapped and nothing else changed. The repetition is the argument: the same shout works in a prison as in a desert.

stichs.en: He brought them out from darkness and deepest gloom,
and snapped their bonds apart.

verses.summary: Release told in two moves, out of the dark and out of the irons, matching the two halves of verse 10 in the same order.

stichs.en: Let them thank the LORD for His kindness,
and for His wonders toward the children of humankind.

verses.summary: The thanksgiving refrain repeated without a single change. Its sameness is how the psalm says these are four instances of one event.

stichs.en: For He shattered doors of bronze,
and cut through bars of iron.

verses.summary: Bronze doors and iron bars are city gate fittings, not cell locks. The release is described as the breaching of a fortification.

stichs.en: Fools, because of the way of their rebellion,
and because of their sins, were afflicted.

verses.summary: The third story. The sick are called fools and their state is tied to their conduct, which makes this the harshest of the four diagnoses.

stichs.en: Their soul loathed all food,
and they came as far as the gates of death.

verses.summary: Loss of appetite is the clinical detail the verse turns on, and these gates answer the broken gates of verse 16.

stichs.en: Then they cried out to the LORD in the distress that was theirs;
from their straits He saved them.

verses.summary: Identical to verse 13 word for word. Nothing about the folly named in verse 17 changes what is required of them now.

stichs.en: He sends His word and heals them,
and delivers them from their pits.

verses.summary: Healing arrives as a sent word rather than as touch or medicine, and the second verb is one of escape rather than cure.

stichs.en: Let them thank the LORD for His kindness,
and for His wonders toward the children of humankind.

verses.summary: The refrain a third time. By now a reader supplies it before it arrives, which is what a refrain is for.

stichs.en: And let them offer sacrifices of thanksgiving,
and recount His deeds with glad song.

verses.summary: This group alone is asked for more than words: the todah offering and a public telling of what happened to them.

stichs.en: Those who go down to the sea in ships,
doing business on the great waters,

verses.summary: The fourth story, and the only group not overtaken by circumstance. They went out on purpose, and for trade.

stichs.en: they saw the works of the LORD,
and His wonders in the deep.

verses.summary: The sailors are the only ones said to have seen anything. Their trouble and their view of God's work are the same weather.

stichs.en: He spoke and raised up a storm wind,
and it lifted its waves high.

verses.summary: The storm is not weather. It is spoken into place, which makes the calm later a reversal of an order rather than a victory over chaos.

stichs.en: They rise to the sky, they drop to the depths;
their soul melts away in the misery.

verses.summary: Sky and depth in one line, and the fainting soul repeats the idiom used of the desert wanderers in verse 5.

stichs.en: They reel and stagger like a drunkard,
and all their skill is swallowed up.

verses.summary: Skill fails before strength does. These are professionals, and the verse removes the one thing that made them professionals.

stichs.en: Then they cried out to the LORD in the distress that was theirs,
and from their straits He brought them out.

verses.summary: The fourth and last cry, with a third pair of verbs. The vocabulary rotates and the structure never moves.

stichs.en: He brought the storm to a hush,
and their waves fell silent.

verses.summary: The noun for the hush is the rare one that appears in the thin silence of 1 Kings 19:12. Rescue here is the removal of noise.

stichs.en: They were glad because it grew quiet,
and He guided them to the harbour they wanted.

verses.summary: Relief comes before arrival. The gladness is at the quiet, and the harbour is named by what they wanted rather than by where it is.

stichs.en: Let them thank the LORD for His kindness,
and for His wonders toward the children of humankind.

verses.summary: The fourth and final refrain closes the four stories. What follows is a different kind of poem with no refrain in it.

stichs.en: Let them raise Him high in the assembly of the people,
and praise Him in the seat of the elders.

verses.summary: Gratitude moves into two public settings, the crowd and the council. Private relief is being made into an institution.

stichs.en: He turns rivers into wilderness,
and water sources into thirsty ground.

verses.summary: The hymn opens with the reversal that costs: water withdrawn. The same verb starts verse 35 and runs the other way.

stichs.en: A land of fruit into salt flats,
because of the evil of those living in it.

verses.summary: The one moral cause given in this section, and it is attached to the land rather than to the people who suffer on it.

stichs.en: He turns wilderness into a pool of water,
and parched land into water sources.

verses.summary: The exact mirror of verse 33, with the two halves traded. Wilderness becomes pool and drought becomes springs.

stichs.en: And there He settles the hungry,
and they found a city to live in.

verses.summary: The hungry of verse 5 reappear and the city nobody could find in verse 4 gets built. The four stories are being replayed as one.

stichs.en: They sow fields and plant vineyards,
and produce a fruitful harvest.

verses.summary: Three farming verbs in a row, all with human subjects. What is given is not food but conditions in which work yields food.

stichs.en: He blesses them and they multiply greatly,
and He does not let their cattle dwindle.

verses.summary: Blessing is counted in heads, human and animal. The verse ends on a negative, which is this psalm's way of saying a good thing holds.

stichs.en: Then they dwindle and are bowed down
by the pressure of misfortune and sorrow.

verses.summary: The turn back downward, and no cause is given for it. The psalm refuses to leave the pattern as a simple reward system.

stichs.en: He pours contempt on nobles,
and makes them wander in a trackless waste.

verses.summary: Two half lines shared with Job 12:21 and 12:24, though which text borrows from which is disputed. The great get the wasteland the poor were pulled out of.

stichs.en: He sets the needy safely high above affliction,
and makes their families like a flock.

verses.summary: The verb is the one used of a fortress out of reach. The flock image at the end puts a shepherd back into a psalm about roads and ships.

stichs.en: The upright see it and are glad,
and all wrongdoing shuts its mouth.

verses.summary: Two reactions to one sight, gladness and silence. The psalm gives wrongdoing a mouth precisely so that it can be closed.

stichs.en: Who is wise? Let him keep these things,
and let them study the kindnesses of the LORD.

verses.summary: A wisdom ending, close in form to Hosea 14:10. The psalm does not finish by praising; it finishes by setting the reader a task.

pardes.body: Four groups, one shape. Desert wanderers in verses 4 to 9, prisoners in 10 to 16, the sick in 17 to 22, sailors in 23 to 32. Each block states the trouble, then the cry, {{6.0}}, then the rescue, then the call to give thanks, {{8.2}}. The cry stands at verses 6, 13, 19 and 28; the thanksgiving at 8, 15, 21 and 31. Only the prisoners and the sick are told why they are in trouble, which means the psalm is not claiming that suffering is always earned. From verse 33 the refrains stop and a hymn takes over: rivers to desert, desert to pools, the great brought low and the poor set high. Verse 43 closes by asking the reader to notice the pattern rather than to sing about it.

Three words repay a slow look. The pair rendered as deepest gloom at {{10.2}} is the word from the valley of Psalm 23, read by some as a compound of shadow and death and by others as a single noun for thick darkness; both readings are current. The word for pits at {{20.4}} is ambiguous in the same way: it can be read as graves, or from a root meaning ruin, so translations split between rescue from the grave and rescue from their own destructive ways. And the calm of {{29.0}} uses a causative of the verb to stand, which is why some render it as stilling the storm and others as raising up a hush in its place. The Masoretic tradition also marks part of the sailors section with the rare inverted nun sign found at Numbers 10:35 and 36; its exact placement here and its purpose are both disputed.

The Talmud in Berakhot 54b reads the four groups as a legal list: four people must offer the blessing hagomel, one who crossed the sea, one who crossed the desert, one who was ill and recovered, and one who was released from prison. The psalm becomes the source text for a still living liturgical practice, said in public after the Torah reading, which is exactly the public setting verse 32 asks for. A second reading, common but not tied to one named source, takes the four as four exiles and the return of verse 3 as the ingathering. Note what the plain text does not say: in none of the four cases is the cry described as prayer, and in none of them are the people said to deserve their rescue.

The psalm is bracketed by one word. It ends verse 1 at {{1.6}} in the singular, His kindness, and returns in verse 43 at {{43.5}} in the plural, the kindnesses, so the forty one verses between them are that single quality broken into instances. In the mystical reading the four descents are not accidents to be avoided but the shape of the movement itself: the wanderer, the prisoner, the sick and the sailor each go down before anything rises, and the storm of verse 25 is spoken by the same voice that hushes it in verse 29. The cry in each block is wordless, a shout rather than a formula, which is read as the point at which a person has nothing left to offer and is answered anyway.
